While some may believe that invasive species do more help than harm to the environment, these plants and animals need to be controlled.

Invasive species can replace plants and other forms of life, as well as damaging food chains by consuming a certain species, decreasing the population of another. “Many species thrive because they outcompete native species for food.” (Source 2, line 19) Many invasive species end up growing too quickly and end up thriving more than the other species that have been living in that area, which causes the native species to suffer due to a lack of food and survival needs. Some times people introduce insects as control for invasive plants, but those insects end up becoming an invasive species as well and damaging more of the ecosystem. “Sometimes, the insects also damage other plant species — they can become invasive species themselves” (Source 2, lines 41–42) In attemps to control one harmful invasive species, another species just as harmful was brought into the environment and caused more harm to other species.

Invasive species can spread extremely fast, not giving the surroundings enough time to adapt to the new life and can start suffering severely due to this rapid change. “... establish populations and invade [crossed out: illegible] new habitats, spreading widely and some times beyond the initial point of introduction.” (Source 3, lines 11–12) Invasive species can be brought in and then take over within a month of arriving in the new ecosystem, hurting the other life around it as it continues to grow and

thrive in its new environment. “Many invaders depress populations of native species, and even threaten some with extinction, by preying on them, competing with them, hybridizing them, infecting them with disease, or changing their habitat” (Source 3, lines 19–21) these invaders compete with natives for their food, and sometimes bring disease that kills most of the population that lived there. These species tend to combine with some surrounding species to spread even more and to increase its population.

While invasive species are harmful to the ecosystem they reproduce in, they can have some positive effects in nature as well. “Minor changes to a new ecosystem — an alien plant attracting pollinators to nearby native plants, for example — might help individuals from a native species without boosting their population numbers.” (Source 1, lines 41–43) Invasive plants can help attract more species where both the creature and the plant benefit - for example, flowers and pollinators. This helps boost the ecosystem as well as other populations in the area. “The much rarer major and massive changes occurred when aliens led to [crossed out: illegible] native species expanding their territory or being saved from extinction” (Source 1, lines 44–46). Many invasive species can give other dying species a boost, and allow them to start thriving and expanding again. This is a rare event to happen, but invasive species are able to help the environment [crossed out: illegible] as well, rather than doing only harm to the ecosystems.

In conclusion, many people believe that invasive species are only harmful to an environment and its

surroundings, others find [crossed out: illegible] some of them to be helpful, and give boosts to other populations as well as the environment. Regardless if they're harmful or not, invasive species need to be controlled and contained in order for ecosystems to continue normally without disturbance, and without potential harm.
